claim.citation: Thompson, D.W. (1917) On Growth and Form, Ch. XV 'On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures', pp. 652-669
claim.text: Birds' (and other hard-shelled) eggs are solids of revolution whose meridian curves form a definite, species-varying family of ovoids, comparable geometrically across species.
claim.primary_source_quote_p652: The eggs of birds and all other hard-shelled eggs, such as those of the tortoise and the crocodile, are simple solids of revolution; but they differ greatly in form, according to the configuration of the plane curve by the revolution of which the egg is, in a mathematical sense, generated. Some few eggs, such as those of the owl, the penguin, or the tortoise, are spherical or very nearly so; a few more, such as the grebe's, the cormorant's or the pelican's, are approximately ellipsoidal, with symmetrical or nearly symmetrical ends ... the great majority, like the hen's egg, are ovoid, a little blunter at one end than the other; and some ... are blunt at one end but characteristically pointed at the other, as is the case with the eggs of the guillemot and puffin, the sandpiper, plover and curlew. It is an obvious but by no means negligible fact that the egg, while often pointed, is never flattened or discoidal; it is a prolate, but never an oblate, spheroid.

dataset_verification.pre_scouted_reason: Dryad live search returned 2 title-relevant dataset(s), top: doi:10.5061/dryad.q8rp3.
dataset_verification.verdict_reason: Both title-relevant Dryad records named in thompson_1917_dataset_audit.json for T1917-034 were fetched (through Dryad's Anubis proof-of-work gate) and contain exactly the claim's variables: cross-species bird egg outline shape. dryad.8kv2b20 (Biggins, Thompson & Birkhead 2018) supplies per-egg meridian-curve parameters (Preston 1953 four-parameter ovoid family c0..c3, normalised to half-length 1) for 1389 eggs of 30 auk + penguin species plus a 10-species range set spanning King Penguin to Pheasant-tailed Jacana, i.e. a direct instrument for 'meridian curves form a definite family of ovoids'. dryad.q8rp3 (Deeming 2018) supplies geometric-morphometric outline PCs (PC1 ~ elongation, PC2 ~ asymmetry) for 181 species in 30 orders together with egg and female body mass, i.e. the cross-species comparability and relative-egg-size variables Thompson invokes on pp. 655-656. No analogue substitution was needed.

planned_tests: Solid of revolution: top vs bottom half-profile RMS of the C126 silhouette and of the museum eggs (axisymmetry residual).

Definite family: Preston (1953) 4-parameter ovoid fit residuals on 1389 eggs; reproduce Biggins' C126 coefficients from the raw photograph; Steiner/Thompson Cartesian-oval r + m r' = c negative control on the guillemot (Thompson p. 654 footnote: 'fails in such a case as the guillemot').
Species-varying: between-species variance fraction (eta^2) and Kruskal-Wallis of Elongation / Pointedness / Polar Asymmetry across 30 species; order-level eta^2 on Deeming PC1/PC2 across 181 species.
Comparable across species: normalised (half-length = 1) morphospace of Elongation x Polar Asymmetry spanning the 10-species range set and Thompson's named forms (owl, grebe, hen, plover, guillemot).
Thompson p. 652 'prolate never oblate': min Elongation over all eggs >= 1.
Thompson p. 655 statement (5): asymmetry increases with egg mass relative to parent (Deeming PC2 vs egg/female mass; Biggins species means).
Thompson p. 658 envelope equation p_n + T(1/r + 1/r') = P: pole-curvature closure of the Preston family; sphere when p_n uniform; sign of the pole tension inference.
